clinical: Acute pancreatitis
Digestive enzymes switch on inside the acinar cells instead of in the gut, so the gland starts digesting itself and becomes inflamed. Gallstones and heavy alcohol use are the most common causes.
Chronic pancreatitis
Long-standing damage destroys acinar cells and replaces them with scar tissue, so too few digestive enzymes reach the gut and fat is poorly absorbed (greasy, pale stools).
Pancreatic cancer
Most pancreatic cancers (ductal adenocarcinoma) start in the lining of the ducts rather than in the acini.
Cystic fibrosis
A faulty chloride channel (CFTR) in duct cells makes the secretions thick and sticky, blocking the ducts so enzymes cannot reach the gut.
Type 1 diabetes
The immune system destroys the beta cells, so little or no insulin is made and blood glucose rises.
Insulinoma
A rare tumour of beta cells that releases too much insulin, causing dangerously low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia).
Scarring in chronic pancreatitis
As acini are lost in chronic pancreatitis, the septa thicken with scar tissue, so the gland becomes firm and shrunken.

keys: Lobule: Acinar cell nuclei
parts.description: Acinar cell nuclei are the round nuclei of the pyramid-shaped serous cells that make up each acinus, the enzyme-secreting unit of the pancreas. They sit near the base of each cell, close to the outer edge of the acinus and away from the apical zymogen granules. In a section, look for a ring of round, dark nuclei at the periphery of each acinus, surrounding a tiny central lumen.

keys: Lobule: Zymogen granules
parts.description: Zymogen granules are membrane-bound secretory granules packed into the apical cytoplasm of each acinar cell, facing the lumen. They store mainly inactive digestive enzyme precursors, such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen, which are carried into the duodenum and activated there. In H&E sections they stain strongly eosinophilic (pink), so they form a bright pink cap at the top of each acinar cell.

keys: Lobule: Acinar cells: basal cytoplasm
parts.description: Basal cytoplasm of acinar cells is the strongly basophilic part of each serous cell, lying nearest the basement membrane. It is packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum, whose ribosomes make the digestive enzymes, and its RNA binds haematoxylin, so it stains blue-purple. In H&E sections this dark basal zone is a useful clue that a cluster of cells is an acinus rather than a duct.

keys: Lobule: Acinar cells: apical cytoplasm
parts.description: Apical cytoplasm of acinar cells is the part of each serous cell facing the acinar lumen, packed with zymogen granules. It is less basophilic than the base, because the rough ER lies mostly at the base and the apex is occupied by the secretory granules. In a section, the apical zone looks pinker than the purple base, giving each acinus a two-tone appearance typical of serous secretory units.

keys: Lobule: Centroacinar and duct cell nuclei
parts.description: Centroacinar and duct cell nuclei are the nuclei of the centroacinar cells and of the intercalated duct cells, the first part of the duct system. These nuclei are pale and fairly flattened or oval, lying in the middle of the small cells rather than at their base. Look for them at the centre of an acinus or along the thin duct, where they are paler than the dark round nuclei of the acinar cells.

keys: Lobule: Centroacinar cells
parts.description: Centroacinar cells are small, pale-staining cells that sit inside the acinus, projecting into its lumen. They form the very start of the duct system, continuing into the intercalated duct, and secrete a watery, bicarbonate-rich fluid that helps neutralise the acidic chyme entering the duodenum. In a section, look for pale cells with no zymogen granules, lying in the centre of an acinus, a feature that is characteristic of the pancreas.

keys: Lobule: Intercalated ducts
parts.description: Intercalated ducts are the short, narrow ducts that lead out of each acinus, continuing from the centroacinar cells into the larger intralobular ducts. They are lined by flattened to low cuboidal cells with pale cytoplasm around a small lumen. Unlike many salivary glands, the pancreas has no striated ducts, so you will not see the tall, striped duct cells here; intercalated ducts are the smallest ducts to look for.

keys: Lobule: Tubuloacinar cell nuclei
parts.description: Tubuloacinar cell nuclei are the round nuclei of the acinar cells in the branched, tubuloacinar secretory units of the pancreas, where each acinus is elongated or divided into short tubular branches. Like the nuclei of typical acini, they sit near the base of each cell, away from the apical zymogen granules. In a section, look for basally placed nuclei in cells that line irregular, branched outlines rather than neat, round profiles.

keys: Lobule: Tubuloacinar zymogen granules
parts.description: Tubuloacinar zymogen granules are the digestive enzyme granules of the acinar cells in branched tubuloacinar units. Like those of typical acini, they are membrane-bound packets of mainly inactive proenzymes, such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen, clustered at the apical pole of each cell. They stain eosinophilic (pink) in H&E, so they appear as pink apical granules that are released into the lumen when the cell is stimulated.

keys: Lobule: Tubuloacinar cells: basal cytoplasm
parts.description: Basal cytoplasm of tubuloacinar cells is the basophilic base of the acinar cells in a branched tubuloacinar unit. It is rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum, which makes the digestive enzymes, and its ribosomal RNA binds haematoxylin, so it stains blue-purple. In a section, this basal zone forms a dark rim around the irregular, tubular profiles of the unit, while the apical part stays paler.

keys: Lobule: Tubuloacinar cells: apical cytoplasm
parts.description: Apical cytoplasm of tubuloacinar cells is the part of each branched acinar cell facing the lumen, where the zymogen granules are stored. Because the rough ER is concentrated at the base, this apical region is less basophilic and looks paler and pinker than the base. Its secretion passes into the lumen and drains through the intercalated ducts into the duodenum.

keys: Lobule: Interlobular duct
parts.description: An interlobular duct is one of the larger ducts running in the connective tissue septa between lobules, collecting secretion from the intralobular ducts. It is lined by simple columnar epithelium, with taller cells than the intralobular ducts, and sits in fibrous connective tissue alongside arteries and veins. These ducts eventually drain into the main pancreatic duct, which opens into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.

keys: Lobule: Duct epithelial nuclei
parts.description: Duct epithelial nuclei are the nuclei of the cells lining the intralobular and interlobular ducts, the channels that carry pancreatic juice towards the duodenum. The duct cells are cuboidal or columnar, so their nuclei lie near the middle of each cell rather than at its base, which helps tell them apart from acinar nuclei. Look for these nuclei arranged around a wider, open lumen than an acinus has.

keys: Lobule: Intralobular ducts
parts.description: Intralobular ducts are small ducts lying inside each lobule, collecting secretion from the intercalated ducts and passing it on to the interlobular ducts in the septa. They are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, taller than the flattened intercalated duct cells but shorter than the columnar lining of the interlobular ducts. In a section, recognise them as small round ducts with a clear lumen among the acini, lined by cells with central nuclei.

keys: Lobule: Intercalated duct branches
parts.description: Intercalated duct branches are the small side channels that join the short intercalated ducts to the larger intralobular ducts, forming the drainage network inside each lobule. Each acinus drains into its own intercalated duct, and these narrow ducts merge as they travel towards the edge of the lobule. Their lining cells are flat to low cuboidal with small, central nuclei, so in an H&E section they are easy to miss among the acini.

keys: Lobule: Beta cells (insulin)
Islet A: outer surface — Beta cells (insulin)
Islet B: cellular section — Beta cells (insulin)
parts.description: Beta cells are the islet cells that make and secrete insulin, the hormone that lowers blood glucose by helping muscle and fat cells take up glucose. They are the largest population of islet cells, making up the majority of each islet, and in humans they are more intermingled with the other cell types than in rodents, where they form a central core. In routine H&E sections islet cells look similar, so beta cells are usually identified by insulin immunostaining.

keys: Lobule: Alpha cells (glucagon)
Islet A: outer surface — Alpha cells (glucagon)
Islet B: cellular section — Alpha cells (glucagon)
parts.description: Alpha cells are the islet cells that secrete glucagon, the hormone that raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to release stored glycogen and make new glucose. They form a smaller population than beta cells, and in humans they are scattered among the beta cells, often towards the islet periphery. Alpha cells look much like other islet cells in H&E, so they are identified by glucagon immunostaining.

keys: Lobule: Delta cells (somatostatin)
Islet A: outer surface — Delta cells (somatostatin)
Islet B: cellular section — Delta cells (somatostatin)
parts.description: Delta cells are the islet cells that secrete somatostatin, a hormone that inhibits the release of insulin and glucagon and also reduces gastric acid secretion and gut motility. They are a small minority of islet cells, scattered among the alpha and beta cells, and they look much like other islet cells in H&E. Somatostatin immunostaining is used to identify them.

keys: Lobule: PP cells (pancreatic polypeptide)
Islet A: outer surface — PP cells (pancreatic polypeptide)
Islet B: cellular section — PP cells (pancreatic polypeptide)
parts.description: PP cells are the islet cells that secrete pancreatic polypeptide, a small hormone that helps regulate pancreatic exocrine secretion and appetite after a meal. They form only a small minority of islet cells and tend to lie towards the islet periphery. Like delta cells, they are identified by immunostaining for pancreatic polypeptide, because they cannot be reliably told apart from other islet cells in H&E.

keys: Lobule: Islet cell nuclei
Islet A: outer surface — Islet cell nuclei
Islet B: cellular section — Islet cell nuclei
parts.description: Islet cell nuclei are the round nuclei of the endocrine cells (alpha, beta, delta and PP cells) that make up each islet of Langerhans. They sit in cords and clusters around the fenestrated islet capillaries, and their chromatin is finely dispersed, which makes them look paler and more evenly stained than the dark basal nuclei of acinar cells. In a section, an islet is recognised by a pale cluster of these nuclei with no ducts or acinar lumens inside.

keys: Lobule: Islet capillaries
Islet A: outer surface — Islet capillaries
parts.description: Islet capillaries are the dense network of fenestrated capillaries that thread through each islet of Langerhans, bringing blood into close contact with the endocrine cells. The fenestrations, small pores in the endothelium, let hormones such as insulin and glucagon pass quickly into the bloodstream. Blood reaches these capillaries from small arterioles, and in a section they appear as thin-walled vessels running between the cords of islet cells.

keys: Lobule: Arteriole
parts.description: An arteriole is a small muscular artery that branches from the interlobular arteries in the septa and carries blood into the lobule to supply the acini and islets. Its wall has a thick layer of smooth muscle and its lumen is comparatively narrow, which separates it from the thin-walled venule. In a section, recognise an arteriole by its round outline, thick muscular wall and relatively small lumen.

keys: Lobule: Venule
parts.description: A venule is a small vein that collects blood from the capillaries of a lobule and passes it on to larger interlobular veins. Its wall is much thinner than an arteriole's, with only a few smooth muscle cells, and its lumen is wide and often holds red blood cells. In a section, look for a wide, thin-walled vessel with a flattened lining and little muscle, which contrasts with the arteriole's thick wall.

keys: Lobule: Insulo-acinar capillaries
parts.description: Insulo-acinar capillaries are the capillaries that carry blood from an islet out among the surrounding acini, forming the insulo-acinar portal route. This route is thought to let islet hormones, especially insulin and glucagon, reach the acinar cells directly and influence their secretion. In a single section they look like ordinary capillaries between acini, so they are recognised only by following their blood flow back to an islet.

keys: Lobule: Connective tissue septa
parts.description: Connective tissue septa are the thin partitions of fibrous connective tissue that divide the pancreas into lobules. They contain collagen fibres, fibroblasts, nerves and blood vessels, along with the interlobular ducts that drain each lobule. The pancreas is enclosed by only a thin fibrous capsule, so these septa are the main internal support and route for its vessels and ducts.

keys: Lobule: Fibroblast nuclei
parts.description: Fibroblast nuclei are the elongated, spindle-shaped nuclei of fibroblasts, the cells that make collagen and other fibres of the connective tissue septa and the tissue around the acini. Fibroblasts in the septa are thin and flattened, so their nuclei are slender, whereas acinar nuclei are round. In H&E sections, look for thin, dark, spindle-shaped nuclei lying between pink collagen bundles.

keys: Islet B: cellular section — Islet capillaries
Islet C: vascular window — Islet capillaries
parts.description: Islet capillaries are the fenestrated blood vessels that run through each islet of Langerhans, a small cluster of hormone-producing endocrine cells. Their endothelium has pores, called fenestrations, that let islet hormones such as insulin and glucagon enter the bloodstream quickly. Islets receive a disproportionately large share of pancreatic blood flow, so in a section the capillaries form a dense, fine network between the islet cells.

keys: Islet C: vascular window — Beta cells (insulin)
parts.description: Beta cells are the insulin-secreting endocrine cells of the islets of Langerhans, and they form the largest population of islet cells. Insulin lowers blood glucose by helping muscle and fat cells take up glucose from the blood. In human islets the beta cells are intermingled with the other islet cell types, so they are usually identified by insulin immunostaining rather than by routine stains. Their destruction in type 1 diabetes leads to a lack of insulin.

keys: Islet C: vascular window — Alpha cells (glucagon)
parts.description: Alpha cells are the endocrine cells of the islets of Langerhans that secrete glucagon, a hormone that raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to release stored glucose. In human islets they are intermingled with the beta cells rather than forming a separate zone. In routine stains they look much like other islet cells, so they are identified by glucagon immunostaining.

keys: Islet C: vascular window — Delta cells (somatostatin)
parts.description: Delta cells are the endocrine cells of the islets of Langerhans that secrete somatostatin, a hormone that inhibits the release of insulin, glucagon and several gut hormones. They are sparse, forming only a small minority of islet cells, and they are scattered among the beta and alpha cells. Because routine stains do not separate them from other islet cells, they are identified by somatostatin immunostaining.

keys: Islet C: vascular window — PP cells (pancreatic polypeptide)
parts.description: PP cells are the endocrine cells of the islets of Langerhans that secrete pancreatic polypeptide, a hormone thought to help regulate pancreatic enzyme secretion and appetite after eating. They are among the least common islet cell types and are scattered among the other islet cells. Like the other islet cell types, they are identified in sections by immunostaining for pancreatic polypeptide.

keys: Islet C: vascular window — Islet cell nuclei
parts.description: Islet cell nuclei are the nuclei of the endocrine cells that make up an islet of Langerhans. They are round and usually relatively pale, and they lie scattered through the islet rather than in the neat basal row seen in the surrounding acini. Recognising these nuclei helps you pick out an islet from the exocrine tissue around it, although the nuclei of the different islet cell types look much alike in routine stains.

keys: Exocrine A · Sectioned acinus — Acinar cell nuclei
Exocrine C · Angled acinar section — Acinar cell nuclei
Exocrine B · Intact acinus — Acinar cell nuclei
parts.description: Acinar cell nuclei are the nuclei of the serous acinar cells that form the exocrine acini of the pancreas. Acinar cells are pyramidal, and their round nuclei sit near the basal end of each cell, close to the basal cytoplasm where the rough endoplasmic reticulum is abundant. In a section the nuclei form a neat rim near the outer edge of each acinus, which helps you recognise the acinus as a rounded cluster around a small central lumen.

keys: Exocrine A · Sectioned acinus — Zymogen granules
Exocrine C · Angled acinar section — Zymogen granules
Exocrine B · Intact acinus — Zymogen granules
parts.description: Zymogen granules are the secretory granules of acinar cells that store inactive digestive enzymes, such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen. They sit in the apical part of each cell, facing the acinar lumen, and stain eosinophilic (pink) in H&E sections. They are released by exocytosis when the cell is stimulated by hormones such as cholecystokinin (CCK) or by the vagus nerve.

keys: Exocrine A · Sectioned acinus — Acinar cells: basal cytoplasm
Exocrine C · Angled acinar section — Acinar cells: basal cytoplasm
Exocrine B · Intact acinus — Acinar cells: basal cytoplasm
parts.description: The basal cytoplasm of an acinar cell is the part nearest the basement membrane, and it is packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum that makes digestive enzymes. Its ribosomes are rich in RNA, so this region stains strongly basophilic (blue-purple) with haematoxylin. It contrasts with the paler apical cytoplasm above it, and this basal staining is a useful clue for recognising serous acini in H&E sections.

keys: Exocrine A · Sectioned acinus — Acinar cells: apical cytoplasm
Exocrine C · Angled acinar section — Acinar cells: apical cytoplasm
Exocrine B · Intact acinus — Acinar cells: apical cytoplasm
parts.description: The apical cytoplasm of an acinar cell is the part facing the acinar lumen, and it is filled with zymogen granules that store the inactive digestive enzymes. It holds relatively little rough endoplasmic reticulum but contains the Golgi apparatus, so it stains paler than the basal region. Look for this pale zone above the purple base when you identify serous acini in a section.

keys: Exocrine A · Sectioned acinus — Centroacinar and duct cell nuclei
Exocrine C · Angled acinar section — Centroacinar and duct cell nuclei
Exocrine B · Intact acinus — Centroacinar and duct cell nuclei
Exocrine D · Open tubuloacinar unit — Centroacinar and duct cell nuclei
parts.description: Centroacinar and duct cell nuclei are the nuclei of the cells at the start of the pancreatic duct system: centroacinar cells inside each acinus and the intercalated duct cells just beyond it. These cells are flatter and paler than acinar cells, so their nuclei look pale and flattened, unlike the round, basal nuclei of the acinar cells. In a section, a pale, flattened nucleus in the middle of an acinus is a useful clue to a centroacinar cell.

keys: Exocrine A · Sectioned acinus — Centroacinar cells
Exocrine C · Angled acinar section — Centroacinar cells
Exocrine B · Intact acinus — Centroacinar cells
Exocrine D · Open tubuloacinar unit — Centroacinar cells
parts.description: Centroacinar cells are the flattened ductal cells that project into the centre of each acinus, marking the very beginning of the duct system. They secrete a watery, bicarbonate-rich fluid that is added to the enzyme-rich acinar secretion. Their presence inside the acinus is a hallmark of the pancreas, and in a section they appear as small pale cells lying within the acinar lumen.

keys: Exocrine A · Sectioned acinus — Intercalated ducts
Exocrine C · Angled acinar section — Intercalated ducts
Exocrine B · Intact acinus — Intercalated ducts
Exocrine D · Open tubuloacinar unit — Intercalated ducts
parts.description: Intercalated ducts are the short, narrow ducts that continue from the centroacinar cells and carry acinar secretion out of each acinus towards the intralobular ducts. They are lined by low simple cuboidal epithelium with small, round nuclei and a narrow lumen. In a section they look like small, pale channels, and they are told apart from the larger intralobular ducts by their smaller lumen and lower cells.

keys: Exocrine D · Open tubuloacinar unit — Tubuloacinar cell nuclei
parts.description: Tubuloacinar cell nuclei are the nuclei of the secretory cells in a tubuloacinar acinus, a branched secretory unit whose elongated, tube-like segments bend and branch. Like the nuclei of simple acini, they are round and sit towards the basal side of each cell, but here they line long, branching walls rather than forming a round cluster. In a section, look for a row of basal nuclei along an elongated, branched profile to recognise this type of acinus.

keys: Exocrine D · Open tubuloacinar unit — Tubuloacinar zymogen granules
parts.description: Tubuloacinar zymogen granules are the secretory granules in the apical part of the branched acinar cells, storing inactive digestive enzymes such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen. They are released by exocytosis into the lumen when the cells are stimulated, for example by cholecystokinin (CCK). In H&E sections they stain eosinophilic (pink) and crowd the apical end of each cell, which faces the lumen.

keys: Exocrine D · Open tubuloacinar unit — Tubuloacinar cells: basal cytoplasm
parts.description: The basal cytoplasm of a tubuloacinar cell is the part nearest the basement membrane, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum that makes digestive enzymes. Its ribosomes are rich in RNA, so it stains strongly basophilic (blue-purple) with haematoxylin. In a branched acinus this basal staining marks the outer edge of each elongated secretory profile, which helps tell tubuloacinar cells apart from the paler ductal cells.

keys: Exocrine D · Open tubuloacinar unit — Tubuloacinar cells: apical cytoplasm
parts.description: The apical cytoplasm of a tubuloacinar cell is the part facing the lumen of the branched acinus, and it holds the zymogen granules and the Golgi apparatus. It stains paler than the basal cytoplasm because it contains less rough endoplasmic reticulum. Seeing this pale zone above the purple base helps you recognise a serous secretory cell in a branched acinus.

keys: Exocrine Collecting ducts — Duct epithelial nuclei
parts.description: Duct epithelial nuclei are the nuclei of the cells lining the pancreatic ducts beyond the acini, namely the intralobular and interlobular ducts that carry secretion towards the duodenum. These nuclei lie in a single layer, and the lining becomes taller as ducts grow larger, moving from cuboidal to columnar cells. In a section, the nuclei help you trace a duct wall, which you can tell apart from acini by its open lumen and absence of zymogen granules.

keys: Exocrine units — collecting duct tree
parts.description: The pancreatic duct tree is the branching network of ducts that collects secretion from the acini and carries it to the duodenum. Its smallest branches are the intercalated ducts, which join the intralobular ducts inside each lobule, and these join the interlobular ducts in the connective tissue septa. These in turn merge into the main pancreatic duct, which opens into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla, usually together with the bile duct.
